**Case Vignette: David**

David is a 68-year-old married European man, a clinical psychologist by profession. He presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, Ellen, who has noticed a marked change in his demeanor over the past three years. David sits with a rigid posture, his hands clasped tightly in his lap, his gaze often fixed on a point just above my shoulder. He speaks in measured, deliberate tones, as if parsing each word for hidden meaning.

The trauma, he reveals slowly, was not a single event but a relationship. For two years, from ages 35 to 37, David was in a romantic partnership with a woman named Claire. He describes her as brilliant, charismatic, and deeply unstable. He was a young psychologist then, full of confidence and a belief in his ability to understand and heal. He thought he could help her. Instead, he became her target.

The abuse began subtly. A sharp criticism of his work, a dismissive comment about his family. Then came the shoving, the grabbing, the slamming of doors in his face. He remembers the first time she hit him—a hard, open-palmed slap across the face after he disagreed with her about a movie. He was stunned, not just by the pain, but by the shame. He, a psychologist, a man who was supposed to understand the human mind, was being physically abused by his partner. He told himself it was an anomaly, a bad day. He stayed.

Over the next year, the violence escalated. She would throw things—books, glasses, a ceramic lamp that shattered against the wall inches from his head. She would corner him in the kitchen, her voice a low, venomous hiss, her hand raised. He remembers the precise feeling of her fingers digging into the soft flesh of his upper arm, the crescent-moon bruises left behind. He learned to read her moods, to anticipate the storms, to walk on eggshells in his own home. He became hypervigilant, a state he now recognizes with clinical clarity but cannot escape.

He ended the relationship after she broke his nose during an argument about his work schedule. He told no one. He was a psychologist; he should have known better. The shame was a physical weight in his chest.

For thirty years, David buried the experience. He married Ellen, built a successful practice, raised two children. He was a good therapist, known for his empathy and insight. He believed he had processed it, filed it away. He was wrong.

Three years ago, his son, a firefighter, came home with a story about a domestic violence call. He described the scene—a woman screaming, a man with a bloody lip, the smell of fear. David listened, his face impassive. That night, he did not sleep. The images came: Claire’s face contorted with rage, the feel of her hand against his cheek, the sound of breaking glass. He felt a surge of adrenaline, his heart pounding against his ribs. He got out of bed and checked the locks on every door and window. He did this three times.

Now, David lives in a state of constant, low-grade terror. He avoids social situations where couples might argue, even playfully. He cannot watch movies with scenes of domestic conflict. He flinches when Ellen raises her voice to call him from another room. He has started to sleep in the guest bedroom because he feels a panicked suffocation when she rolls over in her sleep and her hand accidentally touches his back.

At work, he finds himself struggling. He used to specialize in couples therapy, but he has quietly referred all his couples to other clinicians. He can no longer sit in a room with two people in conflict without feeling his own throat tighten, without his own body preparing for a blow. He has become a master of avoidance, a skill he now deploys against his own life. He is a prisoner of a past he thought he had escaped, a psychologist who cannot heal the wound he is most ashamed to name.
